Short answer: I wouldn't simply wait — but I also wouldn't walk into your first AGM brandishing a contribution hike. I'd use the year, not lose it. There's a version of "waiting" that's legitimate (getting numbers you don't yet have), and a version that's avoidance wearing a sensible face. Make sure you choose the first.

**Why "one more year" costs more than it looks**

- Construction inflation has run 3–5% in recent years. On a combined roof + heating package — for 14 units, realistically in the CHF 0.7–1.2 M range depending on choices — a year of delay adds tens of thousands, *plus* another year of an underfunded Erneuerungsfonds. The "savings" from waiting are negative.
- Canton Zurich: when a fossil heating reaches end of life, the replacement must now be largely renewable (heat pump, geothermal probes, Fernwärme), with an Energiereportage required first. Planners and drillers are booked out months to years. Waiting a year doesn't buy a year of calm; it compresses the project into a rushed window later.
- A 1989 roof and heating don't fail on schedule. A leak or a dead boiler in January converts a plannable project into an emergency — the most expensive version, and the worst one for fixed incomes.
- Your own position: since the 2023 revision of the stockwerkeigentum law, the Verwaltung must keep a maintenance plan of at least 20 years and finance the renewal fund accordingly. If you serve unpaid you're liable mainly for gross negligence or intent — but "we all preferred peace" isn't a defence. If the assembly votes to wait anyway, have your warning minuted. That protects you and gives the community a memory.

**Understand what the retirees are actually defending**

Their fear isn't the roof; it's "can I still afford my flat?" The paradox is that the *worst* outcome for someone on a pension is an unplanned special levy or an emergency bill. Steady, moderate, predictable contributions are the kindest version of exactly the same total cost. And the money isn't spent — it moves into a pot they co-own, and it shows up in the sale price when they eventually sell. Buyers' banks now scrutinise the fund and maintenance plan; a thin fund next to two looming projects discounts the price more than the contributions ever cost. The owners quietly hoping to sell "before it hits" are the ones waiting harms most.

**What I'd do in your first 12 months**

1. **Listen first (months 1–2).** Fourteen units is small enough for a one-to-one round, starting with the loudest three. Ask what they fear, not what they want. Often the real block is one specific past decision or one household's liquidity fear — not the principle.
2. **Buy facts (months 2–4).** Commission an independent Zustandsanalyse with a 20-year Unterhaltsplan (roughly CHF 8–15k at this size; ask the cantonal energy advisory about subsidies). Have them check for tar/PAH in the old roof membranes and asbestos — common in 1989 and it moves the budget. Neutral numbers end the "everyone says" era. They may also tell you the 5-year estimate is wrong in either direction.
3. **Build an options menu (months 4–6).** Three scenarios: full pre-funding over 5 years; partial funding plus Darlehen (loans to the community are now explicitly codified — bank or cash-rich owners, repaid over 10–15 years); minimal fund plus special levy at works time. Show the monthly per-flat cost of each over ten years, not the headline sum. In parallel: ask Stadtwerk Winterthur about Fernwärme feasibility (their network is largely renewable — simplest compliant option if a line is near) and pre-check geothermal viability with the canton.
4. **Form a working group including one skeptic.** Co-authored plans pass; delivered plans get filibustered.
5. **Decide at a dedicated Sonderversammlung** once the numbers exist: adopt the plan, adopt a step-up schedule (moderate start, rising over two or three budgets), mandate detailed projects — roof in ~2–3 years, heating ~4–6. Routine renewals need only a simple majority of value votes; check your Reglement for higher quorums.

**At the next AGM, convert the wait instead of fighting it.** Three motions: approve the Zustandsanalyse mandate; approve a first, modest fund increase now (it starts compounding and signals seriousness); fix a decision date with the numbers on the table. Then, whatever the mood, minute the Verwaltung's warning about continued underfunding.

And a line you're free to steal: *"I hear that higher contributions are frightening — mine too. So my job is to make sure this community never gets surprised by a bill. We'll wait for the numbers, not for the emergency."*

Real peace in a Stockwerkeigentümergemeinschaft doesn't come from postponing the hard vote; it comes from a process everyone agrees was fair. The anger in the room is mostly about the last decade of underfunding — don't inherit it as your guilt, inherit it as your mandate.

If you share the fund balance, the current monthly contribution per share, and what the heating runs on, I'm happy to sketch the actual scenarios in numbers.

The case law (BGE) has established that the maintenance plan must cover at least 20 years and that the Erneuerungsfonds must be built up adequately — the fund should not be systematically underfunded. If fund contributions are too low, the Verwaltung is liable (Art. 712a Abs. 3 ZGB: liability of Verwaltung/Verwalter for damage caused by intentional or negligent failure of duties).

2. A 1989 building: roof (the original roof will be ~35+ years old by the time of renewal; typical flat roof lifespan 25-40 years depending on material; if it was renewed once already maybe not).
